content: Babies who are switched at birth are infants who, due to either human error or intentional wrongdoing, are exchanged with one another at the time of birth or shortly thereafter. This results in the babies being unknowingly raised by parents who are not their biological parents. In reality, such occurrences are exceedingly rare, though there have been a few documented or alleged cases. However, the concept of babies being switched at birth is a recurring and popular trope in fictional narratives. As a literary plot device, the theme of babies being switched at birth or in their cradles has been a staple in American fiction since the 18th century. It is a hallmark of melodrama, characterized by improbable situations that are unlikely to occur in real life. This plot device has been consistently used over time. For instance, it was employed in works such as W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan's operas H.M.S. Pinafore and The Gondoliers, where babies of noble birth were switched with those of commoners. Mark Twain also utilized this device in his 1893 novel The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson, where a white baby and a Black baby were switched at birth, leading to both being raised as members of racial groups to which they did not biologically belong. This theme became a frequent element in made-for-TV movies during the 1970s and 1980s and has remained popular in the 1990s and 21st century. Examples include its use in the television series Veronica Mars (involving the characters Cindy Mac Mackenzie and Madison Sinclair), Neighbours (with the characters Bree Timmins and Anne Baxter), and The Young and the Restless (involving characters such as Cane Ashby, Phillip Chancellor III, and the children of Lauren Fenmore Baldwin and Sheila Carter). While this plot device is common in soap operas, it is not as prevalent as the theme of questionable paternity. According to Mumford, this is because the potential causes of questionable paternity are more varied and expansive than those of questionable maternity, which is typically limited to errors or malfeasance leading to babies being switched at or after birth. Questionable paternity, on the other hand, can involve scenarios such as a woman deliberately attributing paternity to the wrong man, unreported rape, or clandestine love affairs. Additionally, it is easier for writers to retroactively introduce questions of paternity into a storyline, whereas introducing questions of maternity after the fact is more challenging. The switched-at-birth trope also appears outside of American fiction, as seen in stories like The Little Michus. In real life, the likelihood of babies being switched at birth is extremely low. However, there have been notable cases that garnered media attention. One such case involved a girl in Wauchula, Florida, who was switched at birth due to a medical error. Her story was later dramatized in the made-for-TV movie Switched at Birth. Another case occurred in South Africa in 1989, where the sons of two women, Margaret Clinton-Parker and Sandra Dawkins, were accidentally switched at birth. The mothers sued the Gauteng provincial government in 1995, seeking damages of ZAR 120,000 each. They were later awarded compensation to cover medical expenses and the projected costs of visiting their biological children. Despite learning of the switch, both families chose to continue raising the children they had been living with as their own. In December 2006, two newborn girls were switched at a hospital in Třebíč, Czech Republic. The mistake was discovered in September 2007 when friends of one of the fathers joked that he was not the biological father of the baby. DNA testing confirmed the switch, and after an investigation, the other family was located. By October 2007, the families were in contact and working on plans to switch the children back. To prevent such errors, hospitals typically take fingerprints, footprints, or palm prints of newborns. Nurses also double-check the baby's identity with the mother, verifying her identity as well, to minimize the risk of mistakes.
